blocks.label: Notice the change while you have time
blocks.content: Look ahead for a change in texture, tire tracks, puddles, or loose material. As you approach, compare what you see with how the bike feels. Keep enough time and space to reduce speed before the uncertain section.

blocks.title: A change in the road
blocks.content:
Two riders approach a stretch that looks different from the packed gravel under their wheels. One keeps the same pace and has to react when the front tire reaches loose stones. The other slows on the known surface, picks a visible line, and crosses without a sudden steering or braking input.

Color alone cannot tell either rider how much grip is available. Shade, moisture, and recent traffic can change the look of the road. Use several clues and leave room to revise your line.

A gravel road can change under you within a few wheel lengths. Packed sections may give way to loose stones, corrugations, sand, mud, or a wet patch. The same road can feel different after rain or grading. Your job is to notice a change early enough to choose a line and speed.

Start with visible clues such as texture, the depth of loose material, tire tracks, standing water, and where the road drains. Then check what you feel through the bars and tires. If the surface is unfamiliar, slow down while you are still on predictable ground. Keep your steering, braking, and pedaling smooth as you cross it.

blocks.title: Read, decide, cross
blocks.description: Use a familiar route at an easy pace before applying this during a ride or race.

steps.detail: Notice texture, loose material, tracks, puddles, and the shape of the road ahead.
Choose the path with room to steer and stop. Do not cross into traffic or ride a blind line to avoid a rough patch.
Reduce speed on the more predictable surface when the next section is uncertain.
Keep your hands on the controls and avoid abrupt inputs. Recheck the line after the front wheel enters the new surface.

blocks.content: During a race, riders ahead enter a pale, loose-looking patch without slowing. Their line may work for their tires and speed, but it is not proof of grip for yours. Leave space, set your own pace, and avoid a sudden move across the road to follow them.

### Four surfaces to recognize

**Packed gravel:** Often feels firm, but a thin loose layer or dust can hide on top.

**Loose stones over firm ground:** The front wheel may wander more than on pavement. Give yourself room, lower speed, and avoid sharp inputs.

**Washboard:** Repeated ridges can make the bike and rider bounce. Choose a manageable speed, keep your arms and legs able to move, and look for a smoother visible line.

**Wet soil, mud, or sand:** Depth and grip vary. Walk a section when you cannot see a controlled line through it.

These are descriptions, not a grip rating. Tires, load, weather, and the ground beneath the surface all matter.

### Tire pressure is a separate setup decision

Record tire size, load, pressure, weather, and surface after a ride. Keep the pressure within the tire and rim makers’ limits. Change one setup variable at a time on a familiar route. Do not treat a color change in the road as a reason to adjust pressure while riding.

blocks.title: Narrate the surface
blocks.description: Practice noticing changes and choosing a line on a quiet route. Speak or mentally name the next surface only when it does not distract you from riding.

variants.label: Short, familiar route with clear sightlines
steps: Choose a quiet route with two or more surface types and room to stop.
Ride at an easy pace. Name a change when you can see it and choose a line before you reach it.
After crossing, notice whether the surface felt as expected. Slow or stop if it did not.
Record one visual clue that helped and one that misled you.

variants.label: Familiar route with a bend or uneven patch
steps: Choose a visible bend or surface change where you can reduce speed on firmer ground.
State your line and where you will slow before you enter.
Cross smoothly and compare your expectation with the feel of the tires.
Repeat only while you can see the route and control your pace.

proof_gate.description: You can identify a surface change early and choose a controlled pace and visible line.
proof_gate.target: On a familiar route, describe the clue, line, and speed decision before crossing a change.

blocks.question: A gravel road ahead changes from packed to loose-looking material. Riders ahead keep their pace. What should you do?

options.text: Match their speed because their tires prove the surface has grip
Look for a visible line, create space, and reduce speed before the uncertain section
Move suddenly across the road to follow the smoothest-looking tire track
Change tire pressure while rolling into the patch

blocks.explanation: Set your own pace on the known surface and choose a line you can see. Another rider’s line does not establish grip for your bike.

blocks.content: On your next gravel ride, note one surface change you predicted correctly and one that surprised you. Record what you saw before each one.
The next lesson covers descending. Use these surface clues to choose your pace and line before the road points down.
